messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

function.name: thermodynamics_calculate_boiling_point
function.description: Calculate the boiling point of a given substance at a specific pressure. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

substance.description: The substance for which to calculate the boiling point.

pressure.description: The pressure at which to calculate the boiling point. This is a float type value.

unit.description: The unit of the pressure. Default is 'kPa'.

message.content:
At 10 kPa the freezing (melting) temperature of pure water is only very slightly above 0 °C – roughly **+0.007 °C** (≈ 0.006–0.008 °C).  

This follows from the Clausius‑Clapeyron relation for the ice–water equilibrium:

\[
\frac{dT}{dP}\;\approx\;\frac{T\,\Delta V}{\Delta H_{\text{fus}}}
\]

Using the standard values at the triple point (≈ 273 K):

* \( \Delta V = V_{\text{liq}}-V_{\text{ice}}\approx -1.63\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3/\text{mol}\)
* \( \Delta H_{\text{fus}}\approx 6.01\times10^{3}\,\text{J}/\text{mol}\)

gives

\[
\frac{dT}{dP}\approx -7.4\times10^{-5}\,\text{K}/\text{kPa}.
\]

From 101.3 kPa (1 atm) down to 10 kPa the pressure change is –91.3 kPa, so

\[
\Delta T \approx \left(-7.4\times10^{-5}\,\frac{\text{K}}{\text{kPa}}\right)\times(-91.3\,\text{kPa})
          \approx +0.0068\,\text{K}.
\]

Thus the freezing point rises by only about 0.007 °C relative to the standard 0 °C at 1 atm. In practice, at 10 kPa water freezes essentially at 0 °C.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?" They want the freezing point of water at 10 kPa. We have a tool to calculate boiling point but not freezing point. But we can approximate or use known phase diagram. At low pressures below 611.657 Pa (the triple point), water will freeze directly to ice without passing through liquid. At 10 kPa (~10000 Pa) > triple point, water can exist as liquid and solid. The freezing point depends on pressure; at 1 atm (101.325 kPa) it's 0°C. At lower pressure, freezing point increases slightly? Actually, freezing point decreases with decreasing pressure? Let's recall: For water, the melting/freezing curve has negative slope: as pressure increases, melting temperature decreases. So at lower pressure, freezing point is higher? Wait, Clapeyron equation: dT/dP = TΔV/ΔH. For melting of ice to water, ΔV = V_liquid - V_ice ~ positive (liquid volume larger). So dT/dP positive? Actually, for water, ice has lower density than liquid, so ΔV = V_liquid - V_ice > 0. Then dT/dP = TΔV/ΔH > 0. That means increasing pressure raises melting temperature. So decreasing pressure lowers melting temperature. So at 10 kPa (< 101.325 kPa), freezing point should be slightly lower than 0°C. How much difference? The slope near 1 atm is about 0.0002 K/Pa? Let's compute: dT/dP ≈ TΔV/ΔH. At 273 K, ΔV ≈ 9.5e-6 m^3/mol? Actually, molar volumes: V_liq ~ 18 cm^3/mol, V_ice ~ 19.6 cm^3/mol? Wait, ice has lower density, so V_ice > V_liq. So ΔV = V_liq - V_ice < 0. Actually, check: density of ice ~ 0.917 g/cm^3, water ~ 1.0 g/cm^3. Molar mass 18 g/mol. So V_liq = 18 g / (1 g/cm^3) = 18 cm^3/mol. V_ice = 18 g / (0.917 g/cm^3) ≈ 19.63 cm^3/mol. So ΔV = V_liq - V_ice = -1.63 cm^3/mol = -1.63e-6 m^3/mol. So ΔV negative. Then dT/dP = TΔV/ΔH. ΔH_fusion ~ 6.01 kJ/mol. So dT/dP = 273 * (-1.63e-6) / 6010 J/mol = -0.000074 K/Pa? Actually, compute: numerator: 273 * -1.63e-6 = -0.000445. Divide by 6010 J/mol gives -7.41e-8 K/Pa. Multiply by 1000 Pa to get per kPa: -7.41e-5 K/kPa. So slope ~ -7.4e-5 K/kPa. So at 10 kPa difference from 101.325 kPa is -91.325 kPa. Multiply slope: -7.4e-5 * (-91.325) = +0.00677 K. So freezing point at 10 kPa would be 0°C + 0.00677 K? Wait sign: dT/dP negative, so decreasing P increases T? Actually, dT/dP negative means increasing P decreases T. So decreasing P increases T. So at lower pressure, freezing point is slightly higher. So at 10 kPa, freezing point ~ 0°C + 0.00677 K = 0.00677°C. So about 0.007°C. So essentially still 0°C. So answer: about 0.007°C.

But maybe they want the freezing point at 10 kPa is around 0.006°C. Provide explanation. Use the Clapeyron relation. Also mention that at 10 kPa, water can still freeze at ~0°C. Provide approximate value.
